other_side: NLW's case is that the selloff is leverage and macro rather than any change in belief about AI, and that the $1.65 trillion of data-centre debt is nothing like 2008. Zitron, nine days earlier, took the opposite side of exactly that argument. His claim is that each data centre is financed through a special purpose vehicle which owns the chips and the debt and services it purely out of customer revenue, keeping the obligation off the parent's balance sheet — "legal, worrying, and yes, a little bit Enron," as he puts it. He accepts the subprime analogy NLW dismisses, calling the paper "poorly-underwritten, virtually-uncollateralized" and noting it now sits with private credit funds, pension schemes and insurers hunting yield. Crucially, he does not need a hyperscaler to default: the losses fall on the vehicles, the neoclouds and their creditors, and because single deals run to hundreds of millions, "all it takes is ten or fifteen of them."
truth_beneath: Both men orbit one variable: whether AI revenue arrives fast enough to service the debt already written against it. They agree on more than either would like — lab revenue is accelerating hard, and roughly $1.65 trillion of data-centre debt sits largely off balance sheet in vehicles the hyperscalers do not guarantee. The empirical question that will resolve is whether contracted compute revenue covers debt service as that capacity energises; the observable that settles it is debt-service coverage ratios and secondary spreads on data-centre securities, plus any missed payment from OpenAI or Anthropic to a neocloud. The residue is pure worldview: whether the demand behind it is real or manufactured. NLW is vindicated if revenue keeps compounding and the paper performs through a rate cycle; Zitron is vindicated if coverage covenants break while the hyperscalers walk away untouched. Both are polemicists with incentives — NLW bullish and anti-doom, Zitron bubble-certain and anti-hype — so the signal is that both now locate the fragility in the financing rather than the technology. Watch the spreads on data-centre paper, not the share prices.
